name: Methylphenidate

lead: Methylphenidate is a prescription stimulant for ADHD and narcolepsy. Reduced appetite and weight loss are among its most common side effects, which is why it is sometimes mentioned in weight-control discussions.
It has not been tested as a weight-loss treatment in healthy people, and its use is regulated as a controlled substance.

paras: It blocks reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine, raising their levels in the brain. The exact basis of its therapeutic action in ADHD is not established.

The US label carries a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction. Other documented effects include insomnia, anxiety, raised heart rate and blood pressure, rare psychiatric events and reduced growth in children. It is Schedule II in the US and Class B in the UK.

lead: Methylphenidate, sold as Ritalin, Concerta and under many other brands, is a central nervous system stimulant prescribed mainly for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy [1][2]. It is a controlled substance in most countries, including Schedule II in the US and Class B in the UK [2].

Its relevance to appearance communities is as an appetite suppressant: loss of appetite and weight loss are among its most common side effects, and some people who obtain stimulants discuss them as aids to eating less. No trial has tested methylphenidate as a weight-loss or cosmetic treatment in healthy people; its weight effects are documented as adverse effects in ADHD patients [2][3].
The US label carries a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction, and lists cardiovascular, psychiatric and blood-pressure precautions [1].

Schedule II (US); Class B (UK); Rx-only in EU

paras: ADHD is the main approved indication, and the drug is first-line in children in most guidelines; narcolepsy is a second indication [2][3]. Off-label uses include treatment-resistant depression and apathy, with weak evidence [2]. Students sometimes use it as a study aid, although a reference summary notes no evidence that it improves grades in people without ADHD [2]. Appetite suppression for weight control is not an approved or tested use.

Appetite suppression and weight loss are among the most commonly reported side effects, and a 2024 systematic review found appetite suppression in children and adolescents [2]. The US label notes that adverse reactions such as weight loss occurred more often in the youngest children [1]. Long-term treatment in children is associated with a mild reduction in height [2].

Common adverse effects include dry mouth, anxiety, nausea, insomnia, abdominal pain, bruxism and small increases in blood pressure and heart rate; rare effects include worsening psychosis and priapism [2]. The label's boxed warning states that misuse can lead to addiction, overdose and death, with higher risk at higher doses or when the drug is snorted or injected [1]. It advises avoiding use in patients with serious structural cardiac disease and is contraindicated with monoamine oxidase inhibitors [1]. A reference summary rates abuse liability as moderate and similar to amphetamine [2].

Methylphenidate blocks the dopamine and norepinephrine transporters, raising extracellular levels of both; unlike amphetamines it is not thought to cause monoamine release [2][4]. The label states that its mode of therapeutic action in ADHD is not known [1]. Imaging studies with PET have used the drug to measure transporter occupancy [5].

Chemist Leandro Panizzon first synthesized methylphenidate in 1944; it was reported as a stimulant in 1954 and approved for medical use in the US in 1955 [2]. Use in children with hyperactivity grew from the 1960s, extended-release Concerta was approved in 2000, and prescriptions rose strongly from the 1990s [2].

No studies have tested methylphenidate for weight loss or appearance goals in healthy people. Trials examine ADHD: a 2018 Lancet Psychiatry network meta-analysis compared ADHD medications, including methylphenidate and amphetamines, across age groups for efficacy and tolerability [6]. A 1971 study compared the subjective and physiological effects of amphetamine, methamphetamine, ephedrine, phenmetrazine and methylphenidate in people [7]. Registered trials cover extended-release formulations in adults with ADHD [8], dermal reactions to a patch [9] and use in epilepsy-related cognitive deficits [10].

timeline.event: Approved for medical use in the US [2].
